structured.name: Vanuatu
structured._source: wikidata (CC0); landBorders + naturalResources from CIA World Factbook (public domain)

prose.hook: Vanuatu is a Y-shaped chain of four main islands and about 80 smaller ones scattered across the South Pacific, roughly three-quarters of the way from Hawaii to Australia. It has no land borders — its neighbors are all sea. Several of its islands sit atop active volcanoes, including some hidden entirely underwater.
prose.physicalGeography: The islands are mostly mountainous and of volcanic origin, with only narrow strips of coastal plain along their edges. This volcanic geology defines the terrain across the whole chain.
prose.climate: The climate is tropical, moderated by southeast trade winds from May to October and bringing moderate rainfall from November to April; cyclones can strike between December and April. Volcanic activity adds to the natural hazards, causing occasional minor earthquakes and tsunamis. Yasur, standing 361 meters, is one of the world's most active volcanoes and has been in near-continuous activity for centuries, alongside other historically active volcanoes such as Aoba, Ambrym, Epi, Gaua, Kuwae, Lopevi, Suretamatai, and Traitor's Head.
prose.economy: Vanuatu is a lower-middle income Pacific island economy that depends heavily on subsistence agriculture and tourism, leaving it environmentally fragile and exposed to shocks — it has been struggling to rebound from the pandemic and Tropical Cyclone Harold, with sizeable inflation along the way. Australia has provided aid for road infrastructure. Its industries include food and fish freezing, wood processing, and meat canning, while exports include fish, ships, perfume plants, wood, and copra. Resources include manganese, hardwood forests, and fish.
prose.peopleAndCulture: Nearly all residents, 99%, are Ni-Vanuatu, with a small remainder of European, Asian, other Melanesian, Polynesian, and Micronesian people. More than 100 indigenous languages are spoken, alongside official languages Bislama, a creole most widely used, English, and French. Protestant denominations make up the largest religious grouping, led by Presbyterians, Seventh Day Adventists, and Anglicans, with a smaller Roman Catholic population and a share of customary beliefs, including the Jon Frum cargo cult.
